subChunks.title: Immunology
subChunks.hookHtml:
“Every second of your life,” Theodora said, “your immune system is making decisions that would be considered extraordinary if performed by a computer: distinguishing self from non-self among billions of molecules, tolerating the trillions of bacteria in your gut while attacking identical-looking bacteria that cross the gut wall into your bloodstream, remembering a pathogen it encountered forty years ago, and coordinating a multi-layered defence across every tissue in your body — all in real time.”

Immunology is one of the most clinically consequential branches of biology. Failures of immune tolerance cause autoimmune diseases (type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus) affecting hundreds of millions. Failures of immune surveillance enable cancer. Exploiting immune memory produced the vaccines that have saved hundreds of millions of lives. And engineering immune cells — CAR-T therapy — is producing some of the most dramatic cancer remissions ever seen in oncology.

At SENIOR level, immunology demands molecular precision: understanding not just what cells do but how receptor-ligand interactions, intracellular signalling cascades, and transcriptional programmes drive immune cell differentiation and function. It also demands critical appraisal of rapidly evolving clinical applications.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Innate Immunity — Rapid, Non-Specific

The innate immune system responds within minutes to hours using germline-encoded pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) that detect pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) — conserved structures shared by entire classes of pathogens (e.g. LPS on Gram-negative bacteria, flagellin, double-stranded RNA from viruses, CpG DNA). Key PRR families: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) — transmembrane receptors on immune cells and endosomes; NOD-like receptors (NLRs) — cytosolic sensors (NOD1, NOD2 detect bacterial peptidoglycan); RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs) — cytosolic RNA sensors activated by viral infections.

PRR activation triggers transcription factor NF-κB and IRF3/7, inducing production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and type I interferons (IFN-α, IFN-β). Type I interferons induce an antiviral state in surrounding cells (upregulation of hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes, ISGs) and promote NK cell and T cell activity.

Complement system: A cascade of ~30 plasma proteins activated via three pathways (classical — antibody-dependent; lectin — mannose-binding lectin recognises microbial sugars; alternative — spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 on microbial surfaces). Converging on C3 convertase, which cleaves C3 into C3b (opsonin — marks pathogens for phagocytosis) and C3a (anaphylatoxin — mast cell degranulation, inflammation). Terminal complement pathway forms the membrane attack complex (MAC) — a pore that lyses bacteria and enveloped viruses.

Adaptive Immunity — Specific, with Memory

The adaptive immune system takes days to respond initially but generates immunological memory — second responses are faster and larger. Its power lies in two features: clonal selection (each lymphocyte carries a unique receptor; only cells whose receptor matches the antigen are selected and expanded) and somatic recombination (V(D)J recombination generates an estimated 10¹⁵–10¹⁸ possible receptor sequences, allowing recognition of any antigen).

B cells and antibodies: B cells produce B cell receptors (BCRs — membrane-bound antibodies) that directly bind antigen. Upon activation (T cell help required for most antigens), B cells differentiate into plasma cells (antibody factories) and memory B cells. Antibody classes (isotypes): IgM (first response, pentamer), IgG (dominant secondary response, most abundant serum antibody, crosses placenta), IgA (mucosal immunity, secreted in saliva/breast milk/gut), IgE (allergy and anti-parasitic), IgD (B cell surface). Antibody functions: neutralisation (blocking pathogen from binding host cells), opsonisation (coating pathogen for phagocytosis), ADCC (NK cells destroy antibody-coated targets), complement activation.

Class switching (isotype switching) — B cells change the constant region of their antibody (from IgM to IgG, IgA, or IgE) in response to cytokine signals from T helper cells, without changing the variable region (antigen specificity). Somatic hypermutation — activated B cells in germinal centres introduce point mutations in their BCR variable regions; those with increased affinity for antigen are positively selected (affinity maturation). This Darwinian selection process within germinal centres over weeks produces increasingly high-affinity antibodies during an immune response.

T cells: T cells recognise antigen only when presented as short peptides bound to MHC molecules on antigen-presenting cells (APCs). This MHC restriction was established by Zinkernagel and Doherty (Nobel Prize 1996). CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells recognise peptides on MHC class I (expressed on all nucleated cells) — they kill virus-infected cells, tumour cells, and transplanted cells via perforin/granzyme-mediated apoptosis. CD4⁺ T helper cells recognise peptides on MHC class II (expressed on professional APCs: dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) — they orchestrate adaptive immunity by producing cytokines that activate B cells, enhance macrophage killing, and regulate CD8⁺ T cell function.

T helper cell differentiation: naïve CD4⁺ T cells differentiate into functional subsets under cytokine instruction: Th1 (IL-12 → IFN-γ production — macrophage activation, intracellular pathogen clearance); Th2 (IL-4 → IL-4/5/13 production — B cell help, eosinophil activation, helminth immunity, allergic responses); Th17 (IL-6+TGF-β → IL-17 — neutrophil recruitment, mucosal immunity, implicated in autoimmunity); Treg (TGF-β+IL-2 → FoxP3⁺ regulatory T cells — suppress other T cells, essential for peripheral tolerance). This master regulator transcription factor FoxP3 is required for Treg identity; mutations in FOXP3 cause IPEX syndrome (immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked) — severe multiorgan autoimmunity.

Vaccines — Principles

Vaccines exploit immunological memory. By priming the adaptive immune system with an antigen (before natural infection), vaccines ensure that upon real infection, the memory response deploys faster and more powerfully than a primary response — typically preventing severe disease. Vaccine platforms: (i) live attenuated (MMR, varicella, BCG) — excellent immunogenicity, long-lasting, cannot be used in immunocompromised; (ii) inactivated whole pathogen (flu, polio IPV, hepatitis A) — safe, usually require boosters; (iii) subunit/protein (hepatitis B, meningococcal, HPV — viral-like particles) — safe, adjuvants often needed; (iv) mRNA vaccines (COVID-19 mRNA vaccines) — mRNA encoding antigen delivered in lipid nanoparticles; cells translate the mRNA and present the protein to the immune system; mRNA is rapidly degraded; no risk of genomic integration; faster to design; highly effective against COVID-19 severe disease.

Immunotherapy — Engineering Immunity Against Cancer

Checkpoint inhibitors: Tumours exploit immune checkpoints — inhibitory receptors on T cells (CTLA-4, PD-1) that normally prevent autoimmunity — to evade immune attack. Anti-CTLA-4 (ipilimumab) and anti-PD-1 (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) antibodies block these checkpoints, unleashing T cell responses against tumours. Response rates of 20–40% in otherwise terminal cancers (metastatic melanoma, NSCLC) with durable responses in subsets. Major side effects: immune-related adverse events (irAEs) — autoimmune colitis, pneumonitis, endocrinopathies — from unleashing self-reactive T cells.

CAR-T therapy: A patient’s T cells are collected, genetically engineered to express a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) targeting a tumour-specific antigen (e.g. CD19 on B cell malignancies), expanded in vitro, and re-infused. CAR-T cells combine antibody-like antigen recognition with T cell killing machinery. Complete remission rates of 80–90% in relapsed/refractory B cell ALL and large B cell lymphoma — remarkable in cancers that were previously almost universally fatal. Serious risks: cytokine release syndrome (CRS — systemic cytokine storm), neurotoxicity (ICANS), and relapse via antigen loss (tumour cells that downregulate CD19 escape).

storyBeats.text: Theodora drew the clonal selection theory on the board — millions of B cells, each with a unique receptor, and a single antigen selecting and expanding a tiny subset. “This is how the immune system achieves specificity without knowing in advance what pathogens it will encounter. It generates diversity first — randomly, blindly — and then natural selection, operating inside your body, selects the useful clones. It is evolution compressed into a lifetime.”
“Checkpoint inhibitors — PD-1 blockers — if you release the brakes on T cells, why doesn’t everyone get severe autoimmunity?”

“Some people do — immune-related adverse events affect maybe 20–30% of patients significantly enough to require immunosuppressants. But our checkpoints evolved because the cost of unchecked self-reactivity was death from autoimmunity. In cancer treatment, you’re accepting a risk of autoimmune side effects in exchange for a chance at tumour elimination. The risk-benefit is often acceptable for someone who would otherwise have weeks to live. For prevention — never.”

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old how a vaccine works at the immune system level — from the injection to the protection it provides against a real infection months or years later. Make sure to explain what ‘memory’ means in the immune system.
learningObjectives: Distinguish innate and adaptive immunity by mechanism, speed, and specificity — including the molecular basis of pattern recognition and V(D)J recombination
Explain the mechanisms of antigen presentation via MHC class I and II, and describe how CD8⁺ and CD4⁺ T cells are activated and differentiate into functional subsets
Describe the molecular mechanisms of at least two cancer immunotherapies (checkpoint inhibitors, CAR-T) including their mechanisms of action, clinical successes, and significant adverse effects

Critically evaluate the principles of vaccine-induced immunity, including how different vaccine platforms generate protective immune responses and the immunological basis for why vaccines sometimes fail
commonMistakes: Thinking antibodies directly kill pathogens — antibodies work by neutralisation, opsonisation, and complement activation; the actual killing is done by phagocytes, NK cells, or the complement MAC

Confusing MHC class I and class II: MHC I (all nucleated cells) presents intracellular peptides to CD8⁺ T cells; MHC II (professional APCs) presents extracellular/endosomal peptides to CD4⁺ T helper cells
Believing mRNA vaccines can alter the genome — mRNA is translated in the cytoplasm and rapidly degraded; it never enters the nucleus and has no mechanism to integrate into DNA

Treating regulatory T cells (Tregs) as simply suppressing immunity — Tregs are essential for preventing autoimmunity (peripheral tolerance) and modulating tumour immune responses; they are not merely immunosuppressive but contextually critical
assessmentCriteria: Can describe the complement cascade — the three activation pathways, the role of C3 convertase, opsonisation by C3b, and the membrane attack complex
Can explain B cell affinity maturation in germinal centres — the roles of somatic hypermutation and positive selection by antigen for high-affinity clones
Can describe CAR-T therapy mechanism (collection, engineering, re-infusion, antigen recognition) and explain cytokine release syndrome as a predictable consequence of the mechanism of action
Can evaluate why vaccines require adjuvants in some platforms and not others, and explain the immunological basis of waning immunity vs durable memory
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A 35-year-old patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presents with kidney inflammation (lupus nephritis). SLE is an autoimmune disease characterised by production of autoantibodies against nuclear antigens (especially dsDNA, histones, and snRNPs). The patient tests positive for anti-dsDNA antibodies and low complement levels (C3, C4).

  1. Explain why loss of immune tolerance to nuclear antigens (self-antigens) might occur — what central and peripheral tolerance mechanisms have failed?
  2. Anti-dsDNA antibodies form immune complexes with circulating dsDNA in the blood. Explain how these immune complexes cause kidney damage.
  3. Why are complement levels (C3, C4) low in active SLE? What does this tell you about the mechanism of complement activation?
  4. The patient is prescribed hydroxychloroquine, a TLR7/9 inhibitor. Explain the rationale for this treatment based on SLE pathogenesis.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Tolerance failure in SLE:
Central tolerance: In the thymus (T cells) and bone marrow (B cells), autoreactive lymphocytes recognising self-antigens with high affinity are normally deleted (clonal deletion) or edited (receptor editing in B cells). In SLE, this process is impaired — autoreactive clones recognising nuclear antigens (dsDNA, histones) escape deletion, possibly due to defects in apoptotic clearance (dying cells releasing nuclear material that activates autoreactive cells) or impaired negative selection.
Peripheral tolerance: In the periphery, surviving autoreactive cells are normally suppressed by regulatory T cells (Tregs), anergy (unresponsiveness due to lack of co-stimulation), or clonal ignorance (antigen not encountered). In SLE, deficient Treg function, excess activation of autoreactive B cells by TLR stimulation (TLR7/9 recognise nucleic acids — aberrantly in SLE via immune complexes delivering nuclear material to endosomes), and impaired clearance of apoptotic material all contribute to the breakdown of peripheral tolerance.

2. Immune complex-mediated kidney damage:
Anti-dsDNA antibodies bound to circulating dsDNA form immune complexes that deposit in the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and mesangium of the kidney — particularly where blood is filtered under pressure and complexes are trapped. Deposited immune complexes activate complement via the classical pathway (IgG binds C1q, initiating the cascade) and activate Fc receptors on local phagocytes and mesangial cells. This triggers local inflammation: release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α), recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages, and complement-mediated tissue damage (C3a, C5a as anaphylatoxins; potential MAC formation). The resulting glomerulonephritis damages the filtration barrier, causing proteinuria, haematuria, and eventual impaired kidney function.

3. Low complement in active SLE:
Complement is being consumed faster than it is produced — active consumption by immune complex-mediated classical pathway activation depletes C3 and C4. The classical pathway (C1q → C1r/C1s → C4 → C2 → C3) is triggered by antibody-antigen complexes; in SLE, the abundance of circulating immune complexes drives persistent complement activation. C3 and C4 are therefore used up (consumed) in the complement cascade. Low C3/C4 with high anti-dsDNA antibodies is a biomarker of active disease flare in SLE. Rising complement with falling anti-dsDNA titres indicates disease remission.

4. Hydroxychloroquine rationale:
Hydroxychloroquine accumulates in lysosomes and endosomes, raising their pH. This disrupts the function of TLR7 and TLR9, which reside in endosomes and are activated by single-stranded RNA and CpG DNA respectively. In SLE, immune complexes containing nucleic acids are internalised by B cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells via FcγR, delivering nuclear antigens (dsDNA, RNA) to the endosomal TLR compartment — pathologically activating TLR7/9 and driving type I interferon production and autoreactive B cell activation. By raising endosomal pH, hydroxychloroquine reduces TLR7/9 signalling, blunting the aberrant innate immune activation that amplifies the autoimmune loop. This is consistent with hydroxychloroquine’s clinical benefit in SLE: reduced flare frequency, lower anti-dsDNA titres, and reduced organ damage over time.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: The COVID-19 pandemic prompted rapid development and deployment of mRNA vaccines (Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2, Moderna mRNA-1273). These vaccines showed ~95% efficacy against symptomatic disease in initial trials and were deployed under emergency use authorisation within 11 months of viral genome sequencing. Some members of the public expressed concerns: that the vaccines were developed ‘too quickly to be safe,’ that mRNA could integrate into DNA, and that the lipid nanoparticles were untested. Evaluate each concern from an immunological and pharmacological perspective, distinguishing legitimate scientific questions from scientifically unfounded fears.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
‘Developed too quickly to be safe’:
This concern conflates speed with corner-cutting. The rapid timeline was achieved by: (i) mRNA vaccine platform technology existed for ~15 years before COVID-19 (cancer immunotherapy, influenza vaccines in trials); (ii) regulatory agencies ran review processes in parallel rather than sequentially with manufacturing; (iii) massive funding allowed phase I, II, and III trials to run simultaneously rather than waiting for sequential results; (iv) extraordinary enrolment speed (>40,000 participants in Pfizer phase III within months) due to pandemic conditions. The standard steps — preclinical testing, phase I/II/III trials, manufacturing scale-up — were all completed; they were compressed in time but not eliminated. Phase III trials were powered for efficacy and adverse event detection with follow-up meeting standard requirements at time of submission. Legitimate concern: long-term follow-up necessarily cannot exist for a new vaccine — rare adverse events with long latency (theoretical) would not be detected in 6-month phase III follow-up. Post-authorisation pharmacovigilance systems (VAERS, Yellow Card, database studies) were specifically designed to detect these. In fact, rare adverse events (myocarditis in young males, mostly mild and self-limiting; VITT with adenoviral vector vaccines) were detected by these systems within months — demonstrating that surveillance worked. Speed of development is not evidence of safety compromise.

mRNA integration into DNA:
This is scientifically unfounded. mRNA: (i) is transcribed from DNA in the nucleus but functions in the cytoplasm — mRNA vaccines never enter the nucleus where DNA is located; (ii) is inherently unstable and is degraded by endogenous RNases within days; (iii) has no mechanism for DNA integration — reverse transcriptase (needed to convert RNA to DNA) is not expressed in normal human cells; (iv) even if reverse-transcribed (which does not happen), integration would require integrase enzyme activity (not present). Some LINE-1 retrotransposon elements could theoretically reverse-transcribe RNA, but this is an extraordinarily rare, non-targeted process that does not result in stable genomic integration at functionally important locations. The biological barrier against mRNA integration is multiple and robust. This concern is not scientifically credible.

Untested lipid nanoparticles:
Partially legitimate but overstated. Ionisable lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery systems had been under development for ~20 years for siRNA therapy — Onpattro (patisiran), the first approved LNP-delivered drug (2018), demonstrated clinical safety. The specific LNP compositions in COVID-19 vaccines were adapted from these platforms. However, the scale of deployment and novel compositions did mean relatively limited clinical experience with these exact formulations in this population before deployment. The PEG (polyethylene glycol) component raised theoretical allergy concerns — anaphylaxis was subsequently detected at ~2–4 per million doses, a rate consistent with other vaccines and manageable with post-injection observation. The concern about LNPs being ‘untested’ is an overstatement; the concern about the specific new compositions having limited prior safety data in general populations was a legitimate (if quantitatively small) uncertainty that post-deployment surveillance appropriately addressed. In conclusion: distinguishing unfounded fears (integration, broad safety compromise) from genuinely limited data (long-term follow-up, specific LNP compositions) is essential for science communication — treating all concerns as equivalent serves neither accuracy nor public trust.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A cytosolic multiprotein complex (most studied: NLRP3) that assembles in response to PAMPs and DAMPs (danger-associated molecular patterns from damaged cells), activating caspase-1, which cleaves pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into active cytokines and triggers pyroptosis (inflammatory cell death). Implicated in gout (urate crystals activate NLRP3), atherosclerosis, and type 2 diabetes.

The phenomenon whereby innate immune cells (monocytes, macrophages, NK cells) can acquire a memory-like state after infection or vaccination — showing enhanced responses to subsequent challenges through epigenetic reprogramming, without specific antigen recognition. Challenges the classical innate/adaptive immunity dichotomy.

The complex cellular and molecular environment surrounding a tumour, including cancer-associated fibroblasts, tumour-associated macrophages (often immunosuppressive M2 phenotype), regulatory T cells, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells — actively suppressing anti-tumour immunity and limiting checkpoint inhibitor efficacy.

The process occurring within secondary lymphoid organs (lymph nodes, spleen) where antigen-activated B cells undergo somatic hypermutation and clonal selection by follicular T helper cells and antigen — producing affinity-matured, class-switched antibodies and long-lived plasma cells and memory B cells.

An engineered antibody that simultaneously binds two different antigens — for example, blinatumomab binds CD19 (on B cell tumours) and CD3 (on T cells), physically bridging tumour cells and T cells to redirect T cell killing against tumours. An emerging immunotherapy platform with multiple approved products.

A heterogeneous group of >450 monogenic disorders of immune function — including SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency, ‘bubble boy disease’, due to ADA or RAG1/2 deficiency), X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (BTK deficiency, no B cells), and chronic granulomatous disease (NADPH oxidase deficiency, impaired phagocyte killing). Study of these conditions has been fundamental to understanding normal immune function.

questions.questionHtml: Which statement correctly describes the distinction between MHC class I and MHC class II antigen presentation?
options: MHC class I is expressed on all nucleated cells and presents intracellular peptides to CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells; MHC class II is expressed only on professional APCs and presents extracellular/endosomal peptides to CD4⁺ T helper cells
MHC class I is expressed only on professional APCs and presents viral antigens; MHC class II is expressed on all cells and presents bacterial antigens to CD4⁺ T cells
MHC class I is encoded on chromosome 6 and MHC class II on chromosome 21 — they are entirely separate genetic loci with no functional overlap
MHC class I and II both present peptides to CD4⁺ T helper cells; CD8⁺ T cells recognise antigen without MHC presentation (via direct BCR-like receptors)
questions.correctAnswer: MHC class I is expressed on all nucleated cells and presents intracellular peptides to CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells; MHC class II is expressed only on professional APCs and presents extracellular/endosomal peptides to CD4⁺ T helper cells
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. MHC class I presents the cell’s internal protein content (endogenous peptides, including viral proteins) to CD8⁺ T cells — enabling cytotoxic T cells to detect and kill infected or malignant cells from inside. MHC class II presents exogenously derived antigens (phagocytosed bacteria, immune complexes) to CD4⁺ T helper cells, which then orchestrate the adaptive immune response.

questions.questionHtml: A patient with HIV has a CD4⁺ T cell count of 180 cells/μL (normal: 500–1500). The patient develops a Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP), a fungal infection rarely seen in immunocompetent individuals. What explains this specific susceptibility?
options: Severely depleted CD4⁺ T helper cells impair Th1-mediated macrophage activation and B cell cooperation necessary for clearing fungal infections — at <200/μL, AIDS-defining opportunistic infections like PJP emerge
HIV destroys CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells, eliminating direct killing of P. jirovecii-infected lung cells
HIV destroys B cells, eliminating antibody production needed to opsonise P. jirovecii for phagocytosis
HIV reduces complement production in the liver, preventing opsonisation of P. jirovecii
questions.correctAnswer: Severely depleted CD4⁺ T helper cells impair Th1-mediated macrophage activation and B cell cooperation necessary for clearing fungal infections — at <200/μL, AIDS-defining opportunistic infections like PJP emerge
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. HIV infects and depletes CD4⁺ T helper cells. Below 200/μL, the adaptive immune response cannot adequately activate macrophages (via IFN-γ, the Th1 cytokine critical for intracellular killing) or support B cell antibody responses. P. jirovecii is normally cleared by alveolar macrophages activated by Th1 cells — without CD4 help, macrophage activation is insufficient. PJP is an AIDS-defining illness at CD4 <200 cells/μL.

questions.questionHtml: CAR-T therapy for B cell ALL typically targets CD19, producing complete remission in ~80% of cases. However, ~20% of patients who initially respond subsequently relapse with CD19-negative tumours. Evaluate why this happens and what strategies could address it.
options: Tumour cells that have lost or downregulated CD19 expression escape CAR-T killing (antigen escape); strategies include targeting multiple antigens (e.g. CD19+CD22 bispecific CARs) or using CAR-T cells that can recognise antigen loss and kill bystander cells
CD19-negative relapse occurs because CAR-T cells are rejected by the patient’s immune system, eliminating the therapy before it achieves lasting remission
CD19-negative cells arise from CAR-T cell toxicity damaging healthy B cells, which then trans-differentiate into CD19-negative cancer cells
The 20% relapse reflects CAR-T cell exhaustion due to chronic antigen stimulation — the CAR-T cells stop functioning rather than the tumour losing CD19
questions.correctAnswer: Tumour cells that have lost or downregulated CD19 expression escape CAR-T killing (antigen escape); strategies include targeting multiple antigens (e.g. CD19+CD22 bispecific CARs) or using CAR-T cells that can recognise antigen loss and kill bystander cells
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. CAR-T cells kill only cells expressing their target antigen. A pre-existing or acquired CD19-negative minority within the tumour is not killed by CD19-targeting CAR-T cells and expands under selection pressure — a form of immune editing analogous to evolutionary selection. Bispecific CAR constructs (targeting two antigens simultaneously), sequential targeting (CD19 CAR then CD22 CAR), or ‘OR gate’ logic CARs are being developed to address this. This is a fundamental challenge of single-antigen targeting in heterogeneous tumours.
